top_level_objectives: Describe how Mars appears to move against the background stars over time, including its temporary retrograde loop.
Compare geocentric and heliocentric explanations for retrograde motion.
Explain retrograde motion as an apparent effect caused when faster-moving Earth overtakes Mars.
Relate Mars’s retrograde behavior to the weaker retrograde loops of Jupiter and Saturn.

scenes.scene_name: Normal Eastward Drift in the Night Sky
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the baseline observation that Mars usually moves slowly eastward relative to background stars.
key_visuals: A nighttime star field with recognizable constellations along the ecliptic
Mars marked across several dates, showing a gentle eastward drift
A timeline spanning several weeks
student_actions: Step through successive nights to track Mars’s position
Identify the normal eastward direction of planetary motion against the stars

scenes.brief_purpose: Show the puzzling observational pattern in which Mars slows, reverses direction, and later resumes eastward motion.
key_visuals: Mars’s plotted path forming a loop or zigzag against background stars
Date markers showing station points before and after reversal
A comparison between the earlier eastward path and the temporary westward segment
student_actions: Advance through the retrograde interval night by night
Mark where Mars appears to stop, reverse, and stop again
Describe why this motion seems surprising from an Earth-based view

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the historical geocentric explanation and why retrograde motion was a major challenge.
key_visuals: A simplified Earth-centered diagram with Mars moving on a deferent and epicycle
The observed loop in the sky displayed alongside the geocentric construction
Labels emphasizing the added complexity needed to match observations
student_actions: Inspect how epicycles were used to reproduce the loop
Compare the geocentric construction to the observed path
Reflect on why this explanation is mechanically cumbersome

scenes.scene_name: Outside the Solar System: Earth Overtakes Mars
scenes.brief_purpose: Shift to a heliocentric perspective and show that both planets move smoothly in their own orbits.
key_visuals: A top-down view of the Sun with Earth on an inner faster orbit and Mars on an outer slower orbit
Motion trails showing both planets advancing counterclockwise
A highlighted moment when Earth passes Mars
student_actions: Animate the orbital motion of Earth and Mars
Identify which planet moves faster and why
Observe the overtaking event from the outside view

scenes.brief_purpose: Link the smooth heliocentric motions to the apparent backward loop seen from Earth’s surface.
key_visuals: A split or toggled view showing the top-down solar system and the corresponding sky path simultaneously
A line of sight from Earth to Mars sweeping across background stars during the pass
The apparent loop building as Earth overtakes Mars
student_actions: Toggle between Earth-based and heliocentric perspectives
Trace how the Earth-to-Mars sightline shifts against distant stars
Explain in their own words how smooth orbital motion produces apparent retrograde motion

scenes.brief_purpose: Reinforce the concept of apparent backward motion using an everyday analogy.
key_visuals: Two cars traveling in the same direction, with the faster car passing the slower one
The slower car appearing to drift backward relative to the faster observer
A visual parallel between the car scene and Earth passing Mars
student_actions: Compare the car-passing analogy to the planet motions
State what is actually moving backward and what only appears to do so
Use the analogy to explain why retrograde is not a real reversal in Mars’s orbit

scenes.scene_name: Comparing Mars with Jupiter and Saturn
scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the concept by comparing retrograde loops of outer planets at different distances.
key_visuals: Side-by-side sky paths for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn during retrograde
A heliocentric view showing their increasingly larger orbits
A visual indication that Jupiter’s and Saturn’s loops appear less dramatic
student_actions: Compare the size and character of the retrograde paths
Relate weaker loops to greater distance and slower apparent angular change
Summarize the general rule for retrograde motion of outer planets
